items.content: The world below arranges itself into something almost unreal from this height — the harbor reduced to a child's toy, the fishing boats threading silver wakes through water the color of hammered glass. Gulls hang level with your shoulders, indifferent, riding currents you cannot feel. The horizon curves faintly, or perhaps you only imagine it does, that subtle reminder that the earth does not end but simply bends away, carrying everything you've ever known along with it.

items.content: The last fireflies of August drifted above the tall grass like sparks that had forgotten how to die, blinking their cold green light against the darkening sky. She stood at the field's edge with her shoes wet from the dew, watching them rise and fade, rise and fade, each pulse a small argument against the coming dark. There was something unbearable about their beauty — the way it belonged so completely to this moment and no other, to this particular end of summer that would never come again.

items.content: Each evening, as the last bruise of daylight faded from the horizon, old Maren climbed the iron stairs with the slow certainty of ritual. She trimmed the wick, polished the great lens until it held the whole dark sea in its curved glass, then lit the flame that would speak to ships she would never see. The light began its turning, patient and mechanical, sweeping its pale arm across the water again and again through the night. She sat below, listening to the fog and the wind, keeping her own kind of vigil.

items.content: Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo.
